title: The Lord's Supper
lead: The meal Jesus gave his followers on the night before he died: bread as his body, the cup as the new covenant in his blood. Christians have eaten it together ever since, under many names.

sections.b: At a meal that Matthew, Mark and Luke present as the Passover (John's timeline places the crucifixion on the day before Passover, John 18:28; 19:14), Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, "This is my body." He took the cup: "This is my blood of the covenant" (Mark 14:22–25; Matthew 26:26–29; Luke 22:14–20). Paul and Luke include "Do this in remembrance of me" (1 Corinthians 11:23–26; Luke 22:19).
sections.refs: Mark 14:22–25; Matthew 26:26–29; Luke 22:14–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26; John 18:28; John 19:14

sections.b: Of the first Christians Acts says, "In one house after another they broke bread, and they shared their meals with joy and with hearts free of pretense" (Acts 2:46). At Corinth the Lord's Supper was part of a full meal, and Paul rebukes the rich who ate first while the poor went hungry (1 Corinthians 11:17–34). Jude 12 calls these meals "love feasts" (agapai).

Christians agree that Jesus commanded the meal and disagree about what happens in it. Catholic and Orthodox teaching: Christ is truly present, the bread and wine becoming his body and blood, and the Eucharist makes present his one sacrifice. Lutheran: Christ's body and blood are truly present "in, with and under" the bread and wine. Reformed (Calvin): Christ is spiritually present and truly received by faith. Memorial (Zwingli, many Baptists and free churches): the meal is a remembrance and proclamation of his death. Each view appeals to Jesus's words in John 6:53–58 ("whoever eats my flesh") and to Paul's "a sharing in the body of Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:16) and "discerning the body" (1 Corinthians 11:24–29).
